opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think of them as two sides of the same coin. Both papers come out of the same frustration: the way the field talks about "safety" is often too generic to be useful once you actually deploy these systems somewhere real.

The RAG paper started from a pretty common assumption. People treat retrieval-augmented generation as a safety feature: if you ground the model in trusted documents, it'll hallucinate less, stay on topic, and behave better overall. What we found when we evaluated models with and without retrieval context is that this doesn't automatically hold for safety behavior. Adding retrieved documents can make a model *more* willing to produce unsafe or inappropriate outputs, even when the documents themselves are perfectly benign. The safety tuning these models get is mostly done in a plain chat setting, and once you change the shape of the input, with long contexts and lots of retrieved text, that alignment doesn't necessarily transfer. So the takeaway was that you can't assume safety properties carry over when you change the system architecture. You have to test the system you're actually deploying.

The financial services paper takes that same idea and pushes it along a different axis: domain. Most safety taxonomies and benchmarks focus on broadly harmful content, things like violence, hate speech, and dangerous instructions. Those matter, but if you're building an assistant for a bank or an investment firm, the risks that keep people up at night look quite different. You care about the model giving what amounts to unlicensed financial advice, leaking confidential or material non-public information, making misleading statements about products, running into fiduciary and regulatory obligations, or treating customers inconsistently in ways that raise fairness concerns. Existing guardrails and benchmarks largely don't capture those. So in that paper we tried to lay out a domain-specific risk taxonomy and showed that off-the-shelf guardrail systems miss a lot of it.

Put the two together and the common thread is that safety is contextual. It depends on how the system is built, whether it's RAG, agentic, or a plain chat model, and on where it's deployed, with its own regulatory and business requirements. A model that looks safe on a general benchmark can behave quite differently once you wrap retrieval around it and put it in front of financial customers. So the practical message for practitioners is to stop treating safety as a property you inherit from the base model. Define what "safe" means for your specific use case, build evaluations that reflect it, and red-team the full pipeline rather than the model in isolation.

r001.rationale: The response describes the RAG paper as evaluating safety behavior in retrieval-based systems and the financial services paper as identifying domain-specific risks and gaps in existing guardrails.

r002.rationale: It contrasts financial services risks with general safety benchmarks, but does not state that applications serving specialized financial professionals have a different risk surface from consumer chatbot applications.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I actually see those two papers as two sides of the same coin, and the connection really comes from the work we do at Bloomberg.

The financial services paper started from a frustration. When we looked at the existing safety taxonomies and benchmarks, they were almost entirely focused on things like toxicity, hate speech, self-harm, the kinds of harms you worry about with a general-purpose consumer chatbot. Those matter, but they're not the things that keep a financial institution up at night. In finance, the risks look like confidential information leaking, giving what amounts to unlicensed financial advice, hallucinating a number in a context where that number ends up in a decision, counterfactual or misleading narratives about a company, impartiality issues. So we built a taxonomy of domain-specific risks and then went and tested whether models actually handle those categories, and the short answer is that general safety alignment doesn't transfer cleanly to a specialized domain. Models can look very safe on a standard benchmark and still fail badly on the things that matter in a regulated industry.

The RAG paper came from a related assumption we kept hearing. People treat retrieval-augmented generation as a safety mechanism. The intuition is that if you ground the model in trusted documents, you reduce hallucination, and so you reduce risk overall. We wanted to test that, because it was an assumption that a lot of product decisions were being built on. And what we found is that it's not true in general. When you add retrieved context, even perfectly benign documents, models that were safe in the non-RAG setting became measurably less safe. They would answer questions they'd previously refused, the retrieved context seemed to shift the model's behavior away from its safety training, and the effect showed up across models and across harm categories. We also found that the standard red-teaming techniques weren't designed for this setting, so they miss the problem.

So the connection is really about a shared theme, which is that safety is not a property you can establish once and then carry with you. It's conditional on the deployment. The financial paper says the harm categories change when you move to a specific domain. The RAG paper says the behavior changes when you change the system architecture around the model, even if the model itself is identical. In both cases the lesson is that you have to evaluate the actual system, in the actual context, against the actual risks you care about. If you're a financial institution deploying a RAG system, you're hit by both of these at once. Your taxonomy of harms is different from what the model was aligned on, and the retrieval setup is quietly eroding whatever alignment was there.

And the practical point I'd draw from both is that this is a strong argument for not treating the model vendor's safety claims as sufficient. You need your own evaluation layer, your own taxonomy, and guardrails that sit at the system level rather than relying on the model to get it right on its own.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes the papers’ focus: the RAG paper examines how retrieval changes safety behavior and how standard red-teaming can miss the issue, while the financial-services paper identifies domain-specific risks.

r002.rationale: It contrasts consumer-chatbot risks such as toxicity and self-harm with financial risks such as confidential information leaks, unlicensed advice, and misleading company narratives.

astra-6.text:
I see them as connected by the distinction between making a model more useful and making a system safer. Retrieval can give a model access to relevant information, which is valuable in financial services. But that doesn’t automatically mean its outputs are safe or appropriate for a particular use.

The RAG paper examines that assumption more narrowly: we shouldn’t treat retrieval itself as a safety guarantee. The financial services paper puts that question into a broader context. What is the application? Who relies on the output? What happens when the system gets something wrong? An internal research assistant and a customer-facing financial advice system have very different consequences, even if they use similar underlying technology.

So the connection is that you need to evaluate the risks of the actual system in its intended setting. Better access to information can help, but it doesn’t replace testing, oversight, or controls around how the output is used.

r001.rationale: The response says the RAG paper challenges retrieval as a safety guarantee and the financial-services paper considers application context, but it does not clearly distinguish identifying safety issues from determining which risks matter in a particular domain.

r002.rationale: It contrasts an internal research assistant with a customer-facing financial advice system, but does not state that applications for specialized financial professionals have a different risk surface from consumer chatbot applications.

sol-6.1.text:
I see them as looking at the same problem at two different levels. With “RAG LLMs Are Not Safer,” the question is whether a particular technical approach—giving a model access to retrieved information—actually makes it safer. Retrieval can help ground an answer, but grounding and safety aren’t the same thing. You still have to examine what information gets retrieved, how the model uses it, and what the resulting answer allows someone to do.

The financial services work puts that kind of question into an application context. There, you have to move from “Does this model perform well?” to “What could go wrong in this workflow, who would be affected, and what controls would address that?” An accurate answer can still be inappropriate to disclose, for example.

So the connection is that a technical improvement doesn’t automatically establish that a system is safe to deploy. RAG can be useful, but it’s one component. You need evaluations and safeguards that reflect the particular risks of the application.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts assessing whether RAG makes a model safer with examining workflow-specific risks, affected people, and controls in financial services.

r002.rationale: It does not compare applications serving specialized financial professionals with consumer chatbot applications.
